wrong: Fingerprint system for filing one finger at a time
That is a single-fingerprint system (such as Battley's), used for latent prints from crime scenes.
Identification system based on body measurements
That is Bertillon's anthropometry.
Classification of palm prints by their creases
Palm prints are classified separately; the Henry system uses all ten fingers.

Options are similar-length expansions of the acronym.

wrong: DNA from the Y chromosome for paternal lineage
That is Y-STR analysis.
DNA from the cell nucleus from both parents
That is nuclear DNA analysis.
Protein markers from red blood cells
That is blood typing (serology), not DNA.
Single Nucleotide Polymorphism typing
That is SNP analysis, a different DNA method.
Restriction Fragment Length testing
That is RFLP analysis, an older DNA method.
Mitochondrial sequence comparison
That is mitochondrial DNA analysis.
Projectile in flight vs. impact on target
That is external vs. terminal ballistics.
Inside gun vs. impact on target
That is internal vs. terminal; external ballistics is the flight.
Firing pin marks vs. extractor marks
Those are marks on cartridge cases studied in firearm identification, not the two branches.
Study of projectile motion in flight
That is external ballistics.
Study of events inside the gun barrel
That is internal (interior) ballistics.
Study of marks on fired cartridges
That is firearm identification from cartridge cases.
Marks from firing pin on primer
That is the firing pin impression on the cartridge case.
Marks from extractor on cartridge rim
That is an extractor mark.
Marks from breech face on case head
That is a breech face mark.
Marks unique to one particular firearm
Those are individual characteristics.
Accidental marks from wear and damage
Wear and damage marks are individual characteristics, not class characteristics.
Serial number stamped by the manufacturer
A serial number identifies one gun's record; it is not a class characteristic of the rifling.
Features shared by one make and model
Those are class characteristics.
Caliber and number of lands and grooves
Those are class characteristics.
Direction of twist of the rifling
That is a class characteristic.

wrong: Testing for cannabis and hashish

Presumptive blood tests include benzidine and phenolphthalein; Marquis is for opiates and amphetamines.

Technique to magnify very small traces
That is microscopy.
Technique to identify blood types
That is serology.
Separating mixtures as they move on a medium
That is chromatography.
Measuring how much light a sample absorbs
That is spectrophotometry.
Examining samples under polarized light
That is polarized light microscopy.
Measuring substances by molecular mass
That is mass spectrometry.
Separating substances on a stationary phase
That is chromatography.
Photographing evidence under ultraviolet light
That is ultraviolet photography.
Analysis using separation on a column
That is chromatography.
Analysis using magnification of samples
That is microscopy.
Analysis using chemical color reactions
Color tests are presumptive chemical tests, not spectroscopy.
Gradual stiffening hours after death
That is rigor mortis.
Stiffening caused by heat exposure
That is heat stiffening, seen in burned bodies.
Stiffening caused by freezing cold
That is cold stiffening.
Determine the cause of death
Vitreous potassium helps estimate the time since death, not the cause.
Determine the victim's blood type
Blood typing uses blood, not vitreous humor.
Determine the victim's age at death

Study of plants found at scenes
That is forensic botany.
Study of bones and skeletal remains
That is forensic anthropology.
Study of soil on shoes and tires
That is forensic geology.
Drying of a body in hot, dry conditions

Purplish color where blood settles
That is livor mortis.
Greenish skin from bacterial action
That is discoloration during putrefaction.
Clouding of the cornea after death
That is corneal clouding.
Pinpoint bleeding in the whites of the eyes
Those are petechial hemorrhages, often seen in asphyxia.
Softening of the eyeball after death

keep: Options are similar-length expansions of the acronym.

wrong: Loops, whorls and arches
Those are fingerprint pattern types, not minutiae.
Cores, deltas and ridge counts
Those are classification reference points, not minutiae.
Pores, edges and creases
Pores and edges are studied in poroscopy and edgeoscopy; creases are not minutiae.
Innermost point at the center of the pattern
That is the core.
Two innermost ridges that run parallel, then diverge
Those are type lines.
Recurving ridge that forms a loop
That is the recurve of a loop, not the delta.
Point nearest the divergence of type lines
That is the delta.
Ridge that forks into two branches
That is a bifurcation.
Count of ridges between two points
That is ridge counting.
Questions about the crime under investigation
Those are relevant questions.
Questions unrelated to anything emotional
Those are irrelevant (neutral) questions.
Questions that accuse the subject directly
Accusing the subject is interrogation, not a polygraph control question.
Comparing responses to relevant and control questions
That is the control (comparison) question technique.
Asking about a detail only the guilty would know
That is the peak of tension, or guilty knowledge, test.
Recording reactions to a series of known numbers
That is the stimulation (card) test.
Differences caused by deliberate disguise
That is disguised writing.
Differences between two different writers
Those are fundamental differences, which point to different writers.
Differences caused by tracing a model
That is a traced forgery.
Writing copied by tracing a genuine model
That is a traced forgery of someone else's writing.
Normal variation in one writer's hand
That is natural variation.
Writing made while ill or very old
That is writing affected by health or age, not deliberate.

keep: Options are similar-length expansions of the acronym.

wrong: Drug breakdown in the liver before death
That is metabolism.
Drug removal from the body in urine
That is excretion.
Drug spreading from blood into tissues in life
That is distribution during life, not after death.
Rate of rigor mortis onset
Rigor depends on temperature and activity, not on drug redistribution.
Accuracy of DNA profiling
DNA profiles are not affected by drug redistribution.
Timing of livor mortis fixation
Fixation of lividity is a separate postmortem change.
Comparing different groups at one time
That is a cross-sectional study.
Studying one case in great depth
That is a case study.
Randomly assigning subjects to groups
That is an experiment.
Crimes solved without any arrest
That is clearance without arrest, not the dark figure.
Crimes recorded in police statistics
Those are the known crimes; the dark figure is what never appears there.
Crimes committed at night
Despite its name, the dark figure is about unreported crime, not the time of day.
Tactical assault to rescue hostages
That is a tactical option, used when negotiation fails.
Bargaining over a plea in court
That is plea bargaining.
Mediation of disputes between neighbors
That is barangay mediation, not crisis negotiation.
Long-term therapy for a mental disorder
Crisis intervention is short-term and immediate.
Police response to a crime in progress
That is emergency police response.
Negotiation with a barricaded suspect
That is crisis negotiation.
Using law strictly by its technical wording
That is legal formalism.
Using punishment to deter future offenders
That is deterrence.
Using mediation instead of court trials
That is alternative dispute resolution.
Repeated victimization of the same person
That is repeat victimization.
Harm caused by the system's response to victims
That is secondary victimization.
State payment to victims of violent crime
That is victim compensation.
Preventing crime in the general population
That is primary prevention.
Preventing crime among at-risk groups
That is secondary prevention.
Preventing crime by target hardening
That is situational crime prevention.
Using tradition to guide prevention
Tradition is what evidence-based practice replaces.
Using public opinion to guide prevention
Popularity is not evidence of what works.
Using more patrols in every area
Spreading patrols everywhere is not evidence-based targeting.
Concentrating on repeat offenders
That is offender-focused policing.
Patrolling all areas equally
That is equal-coverage patrol, the opposite of hot spots policing.
Concentrating on traffic violations
That is traffic enforcement.
Harm caused directly by the offender
That is primary victimization.
Harm to people close to the victim
That is indirect (tertiary) victimization.
Harm from being victimized repeatedly
That is repeat victimization.

Public fear of punishment by authorities
Fear is deterrence; legitimacy is willing acceptance of authority.
Number of officers per population served

Supervision, Commitment, Involvement, Values
Hirschi's four bonds are attachment, commitment, involvement and belief.
Crime from blocked access to goals
That is strain theory.
Crime from weak attachment to others
That is social bond theory.
Crime from a chosen rational calculation
That is rational choice theory.
Crime from learning with intimate groups
That is differential association.
Crime from weak bonds to conventional society
That is social bond theory.
Crime from society's reaction to deviance
That is labeling theory.
Blocked opportunities lead to crime
That is strain theory.
Learned definitions lead to crime
That is differential association.
Labels from society lead to crime
That is labeling theory.

Those are investigative concepts, not the three elements of routine activity theory.
Crime needs weak bonds, strain, peers
That mixes other theories; routine activity names a target, an offender and no capable guardian.
Crime needs a victim, a law, a penalty
Those relate to the legal definition of crime, not routine activity theory.
